extracted.intended_audience: aspiring writers, literary critics, and educated readers interested in literary taste and composition
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical criteria for recognizing and cultivating greatness in literary writing — distinguishing natural, untutored genius from disciplined, art-formed genius and advising on stylistic, moral, and consolatory choices in writing. Drawn from 18th‑century essayistic literary criticism and moral reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great natural genius (untrained, original force)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those few writers who, 'by the meer Strength of natural Parts, and without any Assistance of Arts or Learning, have produced Works that were the Delight of their own Times, and the Wonder of Posterity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristics: nobly wild, extravagant, a 'divine Impulse' that raises the mind above itself; examples given: Homer, some Old Testament passages, Shakespeare, Pindar. Praise: natural force can be infinitely more beautiful than polish. Caution: such writers often fail in nicety/correctness (odd or indecent similes) and may be open to ridicule by lesser wits who notice those failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bienséance / decency and nicety of comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe the rule of decency in allusions and comparisons (what the French call the 'Bienséance').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern refinement values 'nicety and Exactness' in comparisons; avoid indecent or grotesque similitudes (examples: Solomon comparing a nose to Lebanon's tower; Homer’s crude similes). This is a stylistic standard for polished writing: likeness is not enough — the comparison must be decorous and fitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplined genius (formed by rules and art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers who 'have formed themselves by Rules, and submitted the Greatness of their natural Talents to the Corrections and Restraints of Art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristics: greatness expressed through order, regularity and finished skill (likened to a rich soil laid out in walks and parterres). Examples: Plato, Aristotle, Virgil, Tully, Milton, Bacon. This is an equally noble mode of genius, differing in manner from purely spontaneous force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of excessive imitation / slavish adherence to models
rubrics_metrics.description: The risk that disciplined writers 'cramp their own Abilities too much by Imitation, and form themselves altogether upon Models.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: producing only second-rate copies of great authors. Advice: imitation of the best is not equivalent to producing a good original; writers should avoid being entirely model-bound and should preserve their own faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid artificial reproduction of irregular genius (Pindaricks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not imitate the irregularities of an original (e.g., Pindar) by applying them as rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: modern 'Pindarick' writers who copy Pindar's singularity by rule produce distortion and grimace without the 'divine Impulse' — they 'strain after the most unbounded flights of Nature' by mere tricks of art. Quoted satirical admonition (Terence): trying to make madness reasonable achieves nothing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peculiar voice and individual originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Great writers almost always have 'something in their Way of thinking or expressing themselves that is peculiar to them, and entirely their own.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for high literary value: cultivate a distinctive manner of thought and expression rather than merely reproducing fashionable models. Few writers who make an extraordinary figure in the world lack a personal peculiarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance of the ancients’ failures when balanced by force
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient writers may commit 'particular Failures' in nicety, allusion or decency, but their greater daring and force can outweigh those faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive standard: when judging powerful, ancient works, weigh the sublime and daring imagination more heavily than lapses in polish. Avoid cavilling at grandeur from a pedantic focus on small indecencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use classical exempla and authorities to illustrate and teach
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ examples and citations from canonical authors (Horace, Virgil, Dryden, Homer, Pindar, Plutarch, Seneca) to make critical points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: grounding arguments in classical exemplars provides authority and vivid illustration; the essay repeatedly uses translations and paraphrases of classical passages to demonstrate types of character, faults, and virtues in writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting consolatory literature: prefer serious exempla of calamity
rubrics_metrics.description: For consoling a heart in grief, authors who give 'Instances of Calamities and Misfortunes, and shew Human Nature in its greatest Distresses' are more useful than those who merely stir up mirth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice for choosing texts to comfort the afflicted: rather than diverting laughter (e.g., Don Quixote), read grave moral authors whose examples fortify the mind; choose according to the temper of the mourner, but serious exempla are generally recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspective by comparison to greater sufferings
rubrics_metrics.description: One consolation is to compare one's troubles with greater misfortunes in the world: 'we shall be comforted by the Comparison we make between our selves and our Fellow Sufferers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compositional device in consolatory writing: use larger-scale examples (shipwrecks, wars, executions) to give proportion to private grief and to elicit resilience through comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion and devotion as means of consolation in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Devotion naturally appeals to minds in affliction and can provide genuine consolation; consolations from reasoned religion are preferable to consolations from 'a wrong Religion' or superficial diversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing consolatory texts, consider the consolatory power of devotion and well-reasoned religious reflection; anecdote and priestly counsel are used to show religion's capacity to assuage love-sorrow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of moral qualities (constancy vs inconstancy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constancy and steadiness of conviction are presented as virtues; inconstancy (especially in religion or party) makes a person contemptible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character-writing guideline: depict steadiness in life’s great articles as admirable, and use inconstancy as a literary marker of weakness or ridicule. Use examples (Horace, Dryden) to model satirical portrayal of inconstancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of vivid, particular detail to render social scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Vivid representation of local customs and characters (e.g., country wakes: wrestling, beaver-hat prize, Tom Short, Black Kate, Betty Welch) brings scenes to life and reveals social dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique for narrative realism: include concrete, local details, specific names, trades, prizes and small comic incidents to animate description and convey communal values (emulation, courtship, reputation). This essay models close observation as an instructional device.
